_comment: Persons obtaining lawful permanent residence counted by COUNTRY OF LAST RESIDENCE against the same people counted by COUNTRY OF BIRTH. A positive gap means more people arrived FROM a country than were BORN in it -- the country served as a waypoint. THE TWO TABLES ARE SEPARATE TOTALS, NOT A CROSS-TABULATION: no individual is traced from a birthplace to a residence, so a surplus in one country CANNOT BE ATTRIBUTED to any particular origin however well the deficits elsewhere seem to match. THIS DOES NOT REACH TEMPORARY VISAS. Every nonimmigrant series -- TN, H-1B, F-1, L-1 -- is published by CITIZENSHIP ONLY; country of birth is not published for any of them, so a naturalised citizen cannot be distinguished from a native-born one anywhere in the visa data. Who holds a given nonimmigrant status by origin has no published answer. THE COMPOSITION MATTERS AND IS BROKEN OUT: Canada's surplus is 55% immediate relatives of US citizens and 23% family-sponsored against only 17% employment-based, and zero in refugees and asylees. A waypoint whose gap sits in family admission is a different phenomenon from one whose gap sits in employment, and the headline total cannot tell them apart. Countries below 3,000 are excluded because the gap is then noise.
source: DHS Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, tables 2 and 3
